nutshell: Atlanta is where commercial country fiddling began: the Georgia Old-Time Fiddlers' Conventions (1913-35) filled the Municipal Auditorium, and Fiddlin' John Carson's June 1923 OKeh record, from the South's first recording session, launched the hillbilly-record industry. The Sacred Harp still lives here: its publisher, the 1852 Chattahoochee Convention and about 20 annual all-day singings sit in the MSA's western counties. Today's scene splits between intown Decatur and Candler Park (the Frank Hamilton School, founded in 2015 by a former Weaver; Eddie's Attic; Friday and Tuesday contras; church coffeehouses running since the 1980s) and a vast suburban belt of church, barn and cafeteria bluegrass jams and modern western square-dance clubs. About 110 verified series meet roughly 200 times a month: about 41 bluegrass jams, 35 square-dance club nights and 32 open mics, but only about 11 Irish sessions and 10 old-time jams. Heritage life is big and suburban: Gwinnett's Korean festivals, Clayton's garba, Clarkston's refugee mosaic and Stone Mountain's Highland Games.

heritage_traditions.tradition: Scottish Highland games, piping and drumming, Scottish country dance, Burns suppers
heritage_traditions.community: Scottish-heritage Southerners (clan societies), plus a large non-Scottish public
heritage_traditions.evidence: 54th Stone Mountain Highland Games held Oct 16-18, 2026 (founded 1972/73), with pipe bands, athletics, Highland dance, clan tents, Scottish country dance platform and evening dances with live fiddle (Mara Shea); Atlanta Pipe Band in its 56th year with Grade 3 and Grade 4 competition units and an Academy for learners 8+; John Mohr MacKintosh Pipes and Drums (1977) rehearses Saturday mornings; RSCDS Atlanta Branch celebrated its 50th anniversary in 2026 with a new book of 26 dances and 14 original tunes; Burns Club of Atlanta (1896) has held a Burns Supper every year since 1898.
groups: John Mohr MacKintosh Pipes and Drums

heritage_traditions.tradition: Irish heritage: St. Patrick's parade, benevolent society, Irish step dance
heritage_traditions.community: Irish Americans and Irish immigrants
heritage_traditions.evidence: Hibernian Benevolent Society (1858, about 130 members) meets the 2nd Thursday monthly in Dunwoody; the St. Patrick's Parade (since 1858, 142nd edition in March 2026) is billed as Atlanta's longest-running event; Irish dance schools such as the Drake School march in it. Irish sessions (e.g. Marlay House, Decatur, Tuesdays) are covered in the Layer 1 file.

heritage_traditions.tradition: Gujarati garba and dandiya raas (Navratri)
heritage_traditions.community: Gujarati and wider South Asian community, North Fulton, Forsyth, Gwinnett, Clayton
heritage_traditions.evidence: ATL Garba Festival 2025 ran 9 nights over 3 weekends (Aug 29-Sep 14, 2025) at Ambaji USA Shree Shakti Mandir, Morrow, with star Gujarati singers (Kinjal Dave, Geeta Rabari, Kirtidan Gadhvi and others); $200 season pass. Navratri 2026 ran Oct 11-19; ticketing guides describe 3,000-8,000 attendees on big nights (attendance figures unverified, low confidence).
groups: many temple and promoter-run Navratri nights in Alpharetta, Johns Creek, Duluth, Suwanee

heritage_traditions.tradition: South Indian classical music and dance (Carnatic music, Bharatanatyam)
heritage_traditions.community: Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayali and other South Asian families, mainly north and northeast suburbs
heritage_traditions.evidence: Atlanta Fine Arts (student-founded 2022) runs an annual Thyagaraja Aradhana (Feb 1, 2025 at Chinmaya Gurukul, Cumming; reported 360+ attendees); Carnatic Vidyalaya (Viji Murali, 23 years); Kruti Dance Academy (founded 1995, founder Dina Sheth has conducted 100+ arangetrams); also Natya Dhaara, Deeksha, Pavithram, Atlanta Nritya Academy.

heritage_traditions.tradition: West African dance and djembe drumming (African diaspora practice)
heritage_traditions.community: African American community, intergenerational; also West African immigrant teachers
heritage_traditions.evidence: Giwayen Mata (formed 1993) runs a bi-weekly Sunday community West African dance class with live djembe orchestra at Moving in the Spirit (classes listed for Nov 8 and Nov 22, 2026) and produces Kwanzaa Freshii every Dec 30; the Afrikan Djeli Cultural Institute's Atlanta African Dance & Drum Festival (East Point) reached its 17th year in July 2026; Pan African Festival (Decatur, 6th annual, Aug 15, 2026) featured Kilombo and Each One Teach One drum and dance groups.

heritage_traditions.tradition: Caribbean carnival (mas, J'ouvert) and steelpan
heritage_traditions.community: Trinidadian, Jamaican, Kittitian, Grenadian and other Caribbean Atlantans, largely DeKalb, Gwinnett, south Fulton
heritage_traditions.evidence: Atlanta Caribbean Carnival parade since 1988 (Memorial Day weekend; May 2026 J'ouvert, mas parade on Peachtree ending at Rodney Cook Sr. Park); Atlanta Caribbean Carnival Bandleaders Association formed 2003, producer since 2005, already advertising 2027 dates (Children's Carnival May 8, J'ouvert May 28, Parade May 29, 2027); Pan People Steelband played the 2026 Pan African Festival; Nugen Steelpan Academy runs graded classes and a community steelband led by a Trinidad and Tobago-born teacher.

heritage_traditions.tradition: Korean traditional percussion (samulnori/pungmul), gayageum, minyo
heritage_traditions.community: Korean Americans, Gwinnett (about 30,000 Korean American residents per Gwinnett County)
heritage_traditions.evidence: Korean Cultural Center (nonprofit founded 2003; Duluth practice hall) lists a samulnori team, gayageum, haegeum, danso and minyo performers and holds samulnori lessons Fridays 7 pm (practices Wed and Fri); a student Korean ensemble played gayageum at DeKalb Schools' Unity Fest in Clarkston (Mar 28, 2026); Korean Festival at Gwinnett Place Mall Sep 19-20, 2026 (organizers expect 100,000+, unverified).
groups: Korean American Association of Greater Atlanta

heritage_traditions.tradition: Chinese classical and folk dance (ribbon, fan, sword)
heritage_traditions.community: Chinese and Taiwanese Americans, Chamblee/Doraville/Duluth/Johns Creek
heritage_traditions.evidence: Atlanta Chinese Dance Company, founded 1991 by Hwee-Eng Y. Lee (teaching in metro Atlanta since 1986, started with five students at the Chinese Community Center in Chamblee); co-directed by her daughter Kerry Lee; staged 'Chinese American Journeys' at Emory in Aug 2026 and performed at the East by Southeast festival, Clarkston, Oct 2026.

heritage_traditions.tradition: Okinawan eisa taiko
heritage_traditions.community: Okinawan Japanese families (Atlanta Okinawa Kenjin-Kai)
heritage_traditions.evidence: Mirai Kanai ('Future's Path') eisa group of the Atlanta Okinawa Kenjin-Kai; JapanFest is its biggest annual show; booked at the Atlanta Botanical Garden (Aug 28, 2026) and the East by Southeast Festival of the Arts (Oct 16-18, 2026).

heritage_traditions.tradition: Vietnamese Tet celebrations and lion dance
heritage_traditions.community: Vietnamese Americans, Buford Highway corridor and Norcross
heritage_traditions.evidence: Vietnamese American Community of Georgia's Tet New Year at the Korean American Center, Norcross (2025 listing); First Senior Center of Georgia (Norcross) Tet festival Feb 2026 with lion dance; attendance figures of 1,200-5,000 reported secondhand (low confidence).

heritage_traditions.tradition: Mexican folk traditions: Dia de los Muertos ofrendas, folklorico, mariachi, El Grito, Danza Azteca
heritage_traditions.community: Mexican and Mexican American community (Buford Highway, Gwinnett, Cobb, Hall-adjacent)
heritage_traditions.evidence: Oakland Cemetery's Dia de los Muertos (4th year in 2025) with the Mexican Consulate and Institute of Mexican Culture: ofrendas, folklorico and mariachi; Plaza Fiesta has hosted the consulate's El Grito for many years (claims 60,000+ attendance; undated page); Danza Calpulli Ehecatl and other Aztec dancers at Stone Mountain's Latino Family Festival and First Voices. No youth mariachi program or Atlanta-based folklorico school could be verified (a search result citing one turned out to be in Lemon Grove, CA).
groups: Consulate General of Mexico in Atlanta / Institute of Mexican Culture

heritage_traditions.tradition: Brazilian samba school (escola de samba) and capoeira
heritage_traditions.community: Brazilian community (concentrated in Marietta/Cobb) and non-Brazilian dancers
heritage_traditions.evidence: Unidos Atlanta Escola de Samba runs beginner/intermediate samba classes, a passista track toward Rio Carnaval, and a 'Samba Saturday: Halloween Edition' on Oct 31, 2026 (bateria classes 'coming soon'); performed at Decatur's 2026 Pan African Festival; Fogo Brasil offers samba, capoeira and percussion.

heritage_traditions.tradition: Cuban casino (salsa) and rueda
heritage_traditions.community: Cuban and Latin dance community
heritage_traditions.evidence: Julian Mejia introduced Cuban-style casino to Atlanta in 1999 at a Sandy Springs studio and has taught it since through SALSAtlanta (ArtsATL, July 2026).

heritage_traditions.tradition: Greek folk dance (church-based youth dance troupes)
heritage_traditions.community: Greek Orthodox parishes (Annunciation Cathedral, Holy Transfiguration Marietta and others)
heritage_traditions.evidence: Annunciation Cathedral Dance Ministry: 75-100 young dancers, weekly Sunday classes in the Hellenic Center (2025-26 year began Aug 3, 2025), adult group meets two Mondays a month, competes at the Hellenic Dance Festival. The Atlanta Greek Festival paused in 2026 for cathedral construction (returns Sept 2027); Marietta Greek Festival advertises its 37th edition.

heritage_traditions.tradition: Native American powwow (intertribal) and Muscogee/Cherokee heritage
heritage_traditions.community: Intertribal Native residents, Muscogee and Cherokee descendants, Lakota and other relocated families, Afroindigenous Atlantans
heritage_traditions.evidence: Stone Mountain Native American Festival & Pow Wow (Oct 29-Nov 1, 2026; 'largest Native American gathering in Georgia'); 36th Indian Springs Native People Festival & Powwow (Sep 5-6, 2026, Butts County); First Voices Festival (5th, Nov 20-27, 2026, Little Five Points; the first powwow inside Atlanta city limits, per organizers); inaugural Atlanta Afroindigenous Peoples Festival (June 14-15, 2025). Reinhardt University's Unity Festival (Waleska) was canceled in 2025.

heritage_traditions.tradition: Atlanta blues (Piedmont/12-string legacy and club blues jams)
heritage_traditions.community: African American and mixed blues community
heritage_traditions.evidence: Lola's Jam, Mondays 10 pm at Northside Tavern ('one of Atlanta's longest-running musical traditions', listed Oct 26, 2026); Atlanta Blues Society (Keeping the Blues Alive award 2019) ran the 2026 Atlanta Blues Challenge and an Oct 18, 2026 gathering and jam at Blind Willie's. The acoustic Piedmont 12-string style of Blind Willie McTell survives mainly as repertoire, not as a community practice (niche).

heritage_traditions.tradition: African American lined-out hymnody and shape-note singing (Black tradition)
heritage_traditions.community: Missionary Baptist congregations, west metro
heritage_traditions.evidence: NEA Heritage Fellow Claude Joseph Johnson (1987; born Douglasville 1913, 'the boy preacher from Atlanta') sang lined hymns and country spirituals unaccompanied with his congregation and recorded 20+ LPs for Savoy in his church. No 2024-26 documentation of Atlanta congregations still lining hymns was found, so current vitality is unverified (low confidence).

heritage_traditions.tradition: Ring shout and praise-house memory (Gullah Geechee related)
heritage_traditions.community: African American artists and descendants; Gullah Geechee migrants
heritage_traditions.evidence: Charmaine Minniefield's Praise House Project recreated a praise house with a ring-shout sound and projection installation at Oakland Cemetery (2021), Emory (Oct-Dec 2023) and Decatur's Beacon Hill (from Mar 2024). The living ring-shout ensemble, the McIntosh County Shouters (NEA 1993), is coastal (outside the MSA).

heritage_traditions.tradition: African American gospel quartet
heritage_traditions.community: Black churches across south and west metro
heritage_traditions.evidence: Celebration of Quartet awards show (Atlanta) keeps the quartet genre visible, and quartet anniversaries are a known Southern church practice, but almost no 2024-26 Atlanta quartet event listings could be verified online.

heritage_traditions.tradition: Appalachian migrant fiddling (Georgia Old-Time Fiddlers' Conventions)
heritage_traditions.community: Rural migrants to Atlanta's mills (e.g. Cabbagetown), north and west Georgia fiddlers
heritage_traditions.evidence: Annual Georgia Old-Time Fiddlers' Conventions in Atlanta 1913-1935 at the Municipal Auditorium; champions included Fiddlin' John Carson, A. A. Gray of Tallapoosa (Haralson County, 4 titles) and Anita Sorrells Wheeler (only woman champion, 1931 and 1934). Living old-time and bluegrass jams continue in the region but are covered in the Layer 1 file; Woodstock Arts presents bluegrass as a 'gateway between North Georgia Appalachia and metro Atlanta'.

heritage_traditions.tradition: Klezmer and Yiddish music
heritage_traditions.community: Jewish Atlantans
heritage_traditions.evidence: Mostly presented rather than community-made: The Breman's 2026 Levison series brought the New Orleans Klezmer All Stars (Mar 22, 2026); Neranenah (formerly the Atlanta Jewish Music Festival) presents Jewish music. The nearest community klezmer band found, Klezmer Local 42, is in Athens (outside the MSA).

heritage_traditions.tradition: Arab music and culture (oud, Lebanese song)
heritage_traditions.community: Arab Americans (Lebanese, Palestinian, Syrian, Egyptian, Yemeni)
heritage_traditions.evidence: Alif Institute (founded 2004 by the Arab-American Fund of Georgia; Doraville area) presented oud master Marcel Khalife and sons at SCADshow (spring 2025) and runs cultural programs.

heritage_traditions.tradition: Filipino heritage dance and Independence Day (rondalla not found)
heritage_traditions.community: Filipino Americans (about 40,000 in Georgia per Makabayan Georgia)
heritage_traditions.evidence: Kalayaan Atlanta Philippine festival June 7, 2025 (Stone Mountain) and annual June 12 gala; Catching Mangoes Dance (founded Dec 2023 by Jacque Pritz) makes Filipino-diaspora dance. No Atlanta rondalla found.

timeline.event: Standing Peachtree (Pakanahuili), a Muscogee (Creek) trading village at the mouth of Peachtree Creek on the Cherokee-Creek borderland, first documented (Gov. John Martin letter, May 27, 1782); it gives Peachtree Street its name.
Creek land cessions (1821-25) open the future metro to white settlement; Cherokee removal follows in 1838.
William McIntosh signs the Treaty of Indian Springs at his inn in Butts County and is killed by Muscogee opponents three months later; the site now hosts an annual powwow.
Georgians B.F. White and E.J. King publish The Sacred Harp.
The Sacred Harp published by B. F. White of Hamilton and E. J. King of Talbotton, west Georgia.
Chattahoochee Musical Convention organized (Carroll Co.).
Hibernian Benevolent Society founded; first St. Patrick's parade.
J. P. Reese (born in Jasper County) composes the Sacred Harp tune "Newnan" (no. 321).
Chattahoochee convention resumes after the Civil War at Mount Zion, Carroll County, and starts keeping minutes; it has met every year since except 1881.
B.F. White dies after a fall in Atlanta; buried in Oakland Cemetery.
Fulton Bag and Cotton Mill opens; Cabbagetown becomes a mill village of mostly Scots-Irish Appalachian migrants (up to 2,600 workers; mill closed 1977).
Burns Club of Atlanta organized (Burns Suppers from 1898; replica Burns Cottage completed 1911).
United Sacred Harp Musical Association founded in Atlanta (1904/05).
United Sacred Harp Musical Association ("United Convention") holds its first session in Atlanta; it now meets in Bremen each September.
Atlanta City Auditorium (5,000+ seats) opens at Courtland and Gilmer streets; later home of the fiddlers' conventions.
Joseph Stephen James of Douglasville chairs the Original Sacred Harp revision, ancestor of the Denson book.
First Georgia Old-Time Fiddlers' Convention, Atlanta Municipal Auditorium (April 1).
Georgia Old-Time Fiddlers' Association organized; annual Atlanta conventions run until 1935.
About 50 fiddlers form the Georgia Old-Time Fiddlers' Association in April and hold the first convention at the City Auditorium; J. B. Singley wins. Debate over straw-beating in contest tunes.
Fiddlers reach an estimated 30,000 people during convention week; Carson performs "Little Mary Phagan" on the Capitol steps.
Convention row over a fiddler using sheet music; printed music banned from the contest.
WSB goes on air (March 15 or 16); Fiddlin' John Carson broadcasts about a week later. On September 18 the Home Town Boys (McMichen, Puckett) debut.
Ralph Peer records Fiddlin' John Carson in an empty Nassau Street building in Atlanta for Okeh (June 19).

June: Ralph Peer (OKeh), urged by furniture-store phonograph dealer Polk Brockman, records Carson's "The Little Old Log Cabin in the Lane" / "The Old Hen Cackled" at 24 (later 152) Nassau Street, the first recording session in the South. The first 500 copies sold out within days and sales eventually reached about 500,000.
Lowe Stokes beats Carson (reported in the Literary Digest; likely inspired Benet's 1925 "The Mountain Whippoorwill"). Tanner and Puckett become Columbia's first country artists (New York, March 7-8).
Columbia (Frank Walker) begins regular Atlanta field sessions, running to 1932.
April 17: first Gid Tanner and His Skillet Lickers session, in Atlanta. November 8: Columbia records Peg Leg Howell ("New Prison Blues").

Peg Leg Howell and His Gang, with Black fiddler Eddie Anthony, record (April 8). Victor's first of five Atlanta trips (1927-29) records Blind Willie McTell (October 18). Scottdale String Band's "Stone Mountain Wobble" issued on OKeh.
Andrew and Jim Baxter (Black fiddle-guitar duo from Gordon County) record "Georgia Stomp" for Victor in Atlanta, October 16.
Skillet Lickers record "Hell Broke Loose in Georgia" in Atlanta, reportedly on October 29 (Black Tuesday).
Lowe Stokes loses his right (bowing) hand to a shotgun blast; he later plays with a prosthetic and bow rig.
Anita Sorrells Wheeler of Cobb County becomes the only woman to win the state championship (again in 1934).
Sacred Harp Publishing Company founded.
Last Skillet Lickers session: "Down Yonder" with Gordon Tanner on lead fiddle becomes the band's biggest seller.
Last Georgia Old-Time Fiddlers' Convention; the emcee blames phonographs, radio and "jazz band music".
Chattahoochee Musical Convention begins meeting at Wilson Chapel near Carrollton, built for it by the Wilson family (there exclusively since 1989).
John and Ruby Lomax record Blind Willie McTell in an Atlanta hotel room for the Library of Congress.
Ahmet Ertegun records McTell for Atlantic ("Atlanta Twelve-String"); Fiddlin' John Carson dies December 11.
Georgia Mountain Fair begins in Hiawassee (outside the MSA): 2,000 attendees in year one, about 100,000 by the 1970s.
Gid Tanner dies in Dacula; grandson Phil and great-grandson Russ keep the Skillet Lickers name alive.
George Mitchell and Roger Brown rediscover Peg Leg Howell in poverty via Shorter's Barber Shop on Decatur Street.
Everett brothers begin playing at the Suwanee family home; Saturday jams follow, music room 1968, barn c.1971.
Twelfth Gate coffeehouse opens; Georgia State Sacred Harp Convention starts c.1965.
Twelfth Gate church coffeehouse founded (to 1974). May 24: Earl Johnson plays his last show at the Stone Mountain Fiddlers' Convention.
Georgia State University starts a folklore curriculum and Foxfire begins; until then folklore was not an academic subject in Georgia.
Atlanta Pipe Band founded (first pipers met in 1967).
Great Southeast Music Hall opens (Oct 30).
First Stone Mountain Highland Games (some sources say 1973).
Great Southeast Music Hall opens October 30 in Broadview/Lindbergh Plaza (Bill Monroe 1973; the Sex Pistols' first US show January 5, 1978).
WRFG Radio Free Georgia on air; Fox's Minstrel Show begins.
WRFG ("Radio Free Georgia") first broadcasts July 30; first Stone Mountain Highland Games, October 20.
Chattahoochee Country Dancers start contra dancing at Garden Hills Recreation Center.
Contra dancing begins at Garden Hills Recreation Center (Chattahoochee Country Dancers, now Atlanta Contra Dance).
RSCDS Atlanta Branch (50th anniversary 2026) and AAFFM founded.
AAFFM founded; first concert Dec 1976.
RSCDS Atlanta Branch founded (50th anniversary in 2026).

First Atlanta Caribbean Carnival parade; National Black Arts Festival's first festival.
Upstage Cafe opens at 515 N. McDonough St., Decatur, the space that became Eddie's Attic; AAFFM fall campout at Hard Labor Creek State Park.
Wayne W. Daniel publishes "Pickin' on Peachtree: A History of Country Music in Atlanta".

Eddie's Attic opens in Decatur.
Eddie's Attic founded in Decatur by Eddie Owen.
Giwayen Mata formed out of community jam sessions.
Kruti Dance Academy founded.
Southern Crossroads, the Smithsonian folklife program of the Olympic Arts Festival, runs free daily in Centennial Olympic Park (July 18-August 4).
Freight Room closes (Jan); An Eclectic Harmony tunebook published in Atlanta.
St. Patrick's parade becomes a multi-group coalition event; Julian Mejia begins teaching Cuban casino.
Dust-to-Digital reissue label founded in Atlanta by Lance Ledbetter (with April Ledbetter).
Hotlanta Squares founded.
Atlanta Caribbean Carnival Bandleaders Association and Korean Cultural Center founded.
Chomp & Stomp founded in Cabbagetown, honoring Carson, Moonshine Kate and Joyce Brookshire.
First annual Emory Sacred Harp Singing at Cannon Chapel (the second was in 2006).
Lanierland Music Park (Cumming, opened 1970 or 1971) closes; last Atlanta Celtic Festival (about 2006).
Comhaltas North American Convention held in Atlanta ('Ireland in Dixie').
Art Rosenbaum's "Art of Field Recording Vol. I" (Dust-to-Digital) wins a Grammy.
Marlay House opens in Decatur; Trad Music Tuesdays begin.
IrishFest Atlanta launched by Irish Traditions Atlanta.
April 6: GSU centennial celebration of the fiddlers' conventions (Wayne Daniel; Georgia Crackers; Skillet Lickers). November: IrishFest Atlanta launched by Irish Traditions Atlanta.
ECD Atlanta forms its first board (bylaws 2015).
Frank Hamilton School founded.
Frank Hamilton School founded in Decatur.
Centennial edition of J. S. James's 1911 Original Sacred Harp celebrated at Emory (February 14); Frank Hamilton School founded in the fall.
Chattahoochee Country Dancers rename to Chattahoochee Contra Dancers.
Deaths of Hugh McGraw (May 28) and Joyce Brookshire (June 4); the contra group renamed Chattahoochee Contra Dancers; the Atlanta Irish Music School closes.
152 Nassau Street (site of the 1923 sessions) demolished for a Margaritaville resort despite a temporary restraining order.

COVID: IrishFest held remotely; Stone Mountain Highland Games go virtual. Phoenix Irish Arts and the Phoenix School founded. William Bell named an NEA Heritage Fellow.

Frank Hamilton School opens in Decatur's Legacy Park with about 70 students.

Contra community lobbies Decatur City Hall over new rent terms; a Georgia State Fiddlers Convention starts in Blairsville (outside the MSA).

Chattahoochee Contra Dancers renamed Atlanta Contra Dance; its "big 50th" draws 486 dancers.

Inaugural Atlanta Afroindigenous Peoples Festival; Reinhardt Unity Festival canceled; US refugee admissions halted, slowing new arrivals to Clarkston.
The Sacred Harp, 2025 Edition published (about 1,200 submissions, about 113 chosen). Contra "Contra Fantasia" 50th-anniversary weekend (250+ dancers). IrishFest draws about 4,000 people in Roswell.

costs.notes: Shape-note singings are free with potluck 'dinner on the grounds'; a collection covers the $15/day Minutes listing fee. Folk coffeehouses run $10 in 2026. House-concert prices not published (donation-based). Contra $15 ($7 students) per Atlanta Contra Dance's Instagram bio (2026). Fiddler's Green asked a $2 donation in 1988 and $3 in 1990-91. Chomp & Stomp, Southern Crossroads and the Grassroots festival were free. Current Fiddler's Green and Lena's Place prices not captured.

summary.notes: Friday contra $15 ($7 reduced); Tuesday contra $10; SCD classes $4-5; jams and sessions free.

surprises: The building where the South's first recording session took place (OKeh, June 1923, 152 Nassau St., Fiddlin' John Carson) was demolished in 2019 for a Margaritaville resort, despite a temporary restraining order. Bristol built a museum; Atlanta built a resort.
Ralph Peer called Carson's first record 'pluperfect awful'; it sold out within days and eventually sold about half a million.

At the 1914 Fiddlers' Convention Carson brought his hound Old Trail to howl along to 'The Mockingbird', and won. The 1913 convention argued over whether straw-beating was allowed; the emcee 'Alec Smart' kept order with a cowbell and a megaphone, and his real name is still unknown.

The convention's most frequent champion, A. A. 'Mule' Gray of Tallapoosa (inside today's MSA), is the least remembered; the only woman champion, Anita Sorrells Wheeler (1931, 1934), called Carson 'a big bag o' wind' for opposing women entrants.
Lowe Stokes of the Skillet Lickers kept fiddling after losing his bowing hand in 1930, and the band reportedly recorded 'Hell Broke Loose in Georgia' in Atlanta on Black Tuesday, 1929.

The Sacred Harp: 2025 Edition, the first revision in 34 years, debuted at the United Convention in Atlanta (Sept 2025) with singers from 35 states and 6 countries; 10,000 copies went out in about six months and the Georgia House passed a resolution honoring the publisher.

B.F. White, compiler of The Sacred Harp (1844), is buried under a magnolia in Oakland Cemetery, and singers go there after conventions to sing to him. Decatur is one of the last places anywhere that sings from J.L. White's early-1900s 'White Book'.

Carroll County holds the Sacred Harp Publishing Company, the 1852 Chattahoochee Convention and the birthplace of Thomas A. Dorsey, 'father of gospel music'. A separate African American seven-shape 'note singing' tradition (United and Associated Note Singers) meets on a Sunday church circuit in the same western counties, with singers carrying suitcases of books.

Frank Hamilton, co-founder of Chicago's Old Town School of Folk Music (1957) and a 1960s Weaver, co-founded the Frank Hamilton School in Decatur in 2015 and was still teaching there in 2026 at about 92; it runs about 45 weekly classes per term, including one on the songs of Decatur's Indigo Girls.

Bluegrass jams swamp Irish sessions: thesession.org lists only 4 sessions within 80 km of downtown, against about 40 verified bluegrass jam meetings a month, held in churches, a family barn (Everett's Music Barn, a Norcross duplex rebuilt in a Suwanee cornfield around 1970), a beer garden and a meat-and-three cafeteria (Matthews, Tucker).
Modern western square dancing out-meets contra and English dancing roughly three to one; one of the busiest clubs is Hotlanta Squares, an LGBTQ+ club dancing two nights a week.
The Tuesday Night Contra runs about half its nights to recorded music and has staged an 'Electro Contra', rare for a mainstream urban series.

The 1970s contra boom happened at the 'Existentialist Church' in Candler Park; 50 years later the same congregation hosts English dancing, WaltzPlay and AAFFM's Fiddler's Green concerts. Atlanta contra dancers coached the wedding-contra scene in The Hunger Games: Mockingjay Part 2.

Roswell Music Jam's founder called Roswell 'the middle of the jam wasteland' in 2022; his first jam drew 8 people, it now draws about 70 and has spawned church-hosted sister jams in Cumming, Woodstock and Fayetteville.

Atlanta's oldest folk concert series run in churches: Lena's Place (since 1983-84) gives each month's door to a different charity, and Fiddler's Green (since 1986) has gone from $3 and a midnight jam to $10 and home by 10.
WRFG co-founder Harlon Joye has hosted Fox's Minstrel Show since 1973 and was still on air in 2026; Sagebrush Boogie has run every Thursday since 1983.

The Sex Pistols played their first US show (1978) at the Great Southeast Music Hall in a Winn-Dixie strip mall, where Bill Monroe had played in 1973 and Steve Martin played banjo before he was famous.
Eddie's Attic's twice-yearly Open Mic Shootout (58 editions) has crowned Jennifer Nettles, John Mayer and Tyler Childers.

The St. Patrick's parade (1858) is older than the 1864 burning of Atlanta and reached its 142nd edition in 2026; the Burns Club (1896) meets in an exact 1911 replica of Burns' birthplace cottage and was founded largely through the pharmacist at whose fountain the first Coca-Cola was served.
The first Native-led powwow inside city limits came only in 2022 (First Voices, Little Five Points); its theater partner adds a $1 'land use fee' to every ticket to fund Muscogee language work.
Atlanta's biggest garba run happens before Navratri: in 2025 a Clayton County temple ran nine nights of top Gujarati folk singers across three late-summer weekends.
Every Georgia county has its own composed fiddle tune (Frank Maloy's 159-tune project), including a 'Fulton County Hornpipe' in B-flat.
Cecil Sharp never collected in north Georgia, and folklore was not taught at a Georgia university until 1966.

No morris, sword or rapper team, Scottish/Cape Breton session, klezmer band, Scandinavian dance or verifiable son jarocho fandango could be found in a 6.5-million metro; the nearest community klezmer band is in Athens.

RSCDS Atlanta (50 years old in 2026) dances mostly in the exurbs (Marietta, Cartersville, Lawrenceville) and offers a no-steps 'Walk Scottish Together' class; its anniversary book adds Atlanta-named dances such as 'Sylvia, Priestess of Atlanta'.
curiosities: Why does a 6.5-million metro sustain only about 11 Irish session meetings a month (two weekly, both Tuesday)? Compare Irish sessions per million across the 20 metros, against Irish-American share and the presence of a Comhaltas hub.

Atlanta was the cradle of commercial old-time music, yet today has fewer dedicated old-time jams than Asheville or Chattanooga. When and why did the lineage break, and did the same happen in other 1920s recording cities (Bristol, Dallas, Charlotte)?
Is the church-hosted suburban bluegrass 'Music Jam' franchise (Roswell to Cumming, Woodstock, Fayetteville) a Sun Belt pattern also found around Dallas, Houston and Phoenix?
Listing decay: many Southeastern Bluegrass Association jam listings were last edited in 2023. How fast do bluegrass-association jam lists go stale in other cities, and what is the real count?
Modern western square-dance club nights outnumber contra nights here. Is that true in every Sun Belt metro, and are LGBTQ+ square-dance clubs aging out more slowly than traditional clubs?

Sacred Harp heartland paradox: about 20 annual all-day singings in the MSA but only 2-3 local practice singings a month. Do non-heartland cities (Chicago, Boston, Seattle, Philadelphia) have more weekly urban singings and fewer all-days?
Has the 2025 Sacred Harp edition measurably raised attendance? Compare registered singers and leaders in the 2024, 2025 and 2026 Minutes.
How many African American seven-shape note singings still meet in 2026, compared with about 52 in 2019, and who is documenting them?

Church-fellowship-hall coffeehouses (Lena's Place, Fiddler's Green) are Atlanta's folk backbone, as Quaker and Mennonite meetinghouses are Philadelphia's. Is faith-community infrastructure the common thread of surviving folk series nationally?
Recorded-music contra: how common is it elsewhere, and does it draw younger dancers than live-band nights?

Metro Atlanta's Hispanic population is large and fast-growing, yet no youth mariachi program, son jarocho fandango or Atlanta-based folklórico school could be verified. Is that gap real, and how does it compare with Houston, Dallas and Charlotte?
How many big metros had no Native-led powwow inside city limits until the 2020s?
Which other US cities held 1910s-30s municipal fiddle conventions, did they all die around 1935, and why did Georgia's state contest move to the mountains (Hiawassee, Blairsville)?
With refugee admissions halted in 2025-26, will Clarkston's Karen, Bhutanese-Nepali and Congolese performance traditions thin out within a decade?
Are WRFG's continuous roots shows (Fox's Minstrel Show since 1973) the longest-running folk radio hosts in any top-20 metro?
data_quality_notes: SUMMARY: Counts are a verified floor as of Oct 2026. Events without 2024-2026 evidence (16, mostly exurban bluegrass jams from stale SEBA and bluegrassjamsnearme listings, plus the two international/Israeli dance groups whose listings are undated) were moved to unverified_events and excluded from headline_stats; a realistic bluegrass figure is 45-55 meetings a month. Annual all-day Sacred Harp singings are counted at 1/12 per month each. shape_note_singings_per_month includes a low-confidence 3.3/month estimate for the African American seven-shape note-singing circuit. Facebook-only jams and heritage ensembles are undercounted. Gospel quartet programs and church hymn traditions could not be counted from the web. distinct_traditions_active = participatory event categories in use + heritage traditions rated thriving/active/niche. Per-part notes follow. WHERE SOURCES DISAGREE: Stone Mountain Highland Games founded 1972 (organizer) vs 1973 (other sources). Lena's Place opened late 1983 (history) vs 1984 (organizer listing). Eddie's Attic dates from 1992, but the room began as the Upstage Cafe in 1988. Irish sessions: thesession.org lists 4 within 80 km, other listings suggest a few more Facebook-only ones. The NEA Heritage dataset lists the Catawba potter Georgia Harris and the Blind Boys of Alabama under Atlanta, which looks like an address artifact; they are not counted as Atlanta tradition bearers. A realistic bluegrass jam figure is 45-55 meetings a month, above the verified 41. [atlanta-trad] Bluegrass jam evidence leans heavily on the SEBA calendar (open-ended weekly or monthly recurrences that keep showing future dates in Oct 2026 even when last edited in 2023) and on an undated SEBA jam list hosted at davidbelcher.net. last_evidence for these is the calendar entry's LAST-MODIFIED date, not proof of a 2026 meeting. Low-confidence items are kept in recurring_events but excluded from the 'msa_high_medium' totals. Freshly verified (2026) bluegrass jams: Everett's, Roswell, Cumming, Woodstock (Bascomb UMC), Fayette, Ormsby's, Red's Beer Garden (via Live Music Junkiez 2026 list). Source conflicts: Marietta Square jam times (4-8 pm vs 6-10 pm); Red's Beer Garden (6-8 vs 5-8 pm); Tucker Sunday jam venue (HearthSide Club vs Colossus Pizza); Roswell bluegrass circles weekly vs every other Tuesday; Kennesaw Square Dealers 1st/3rd/5th (MASDA) vs 1st/3rd (GSSDA). Several sites block scripted fetches (Marlay House, Ormsby's, israelidances.com, Atlanta Jewish Times, the morris wiki), so a few facts rest on search-engine summaries of those pages; flagged medium/low. Israeli/international folk dance (Machol Atlanta, AIFD) has no dated 2024-26 evidence; kept at low confidence. AIFD may be the same people as Machol Atlanta. No evidence found for: Scottish/Cape Breton sessions, klezmer or Balkan jams, Scandinavian dance, morris/sword/rapper teams, or a regular céilí/set-dance night (only IrishFest's annual céilí and Phoenix classes). 'Not found' was checked with several searches each, but a small Facebook-only group could have been missed. Facebook pages could not be read (login wall); event-level Facebook evidence is limited to search snippets. MWSD club venues are mostly not published on the MASDA/GSSDA lists; lat/lng only given where thesession.org supplied coordinates. The web search tool was heavily rate-limited (shared quota) during this run, so suburban jam coverage (south and east metro: Griffin, Covington, Conyers, McDonough, Carrollton) is thinner than the north-side coverage. [atlanta-song] Shape-note data are strong: atlantasacredharp.org (Annual page updated Sep 2026, monthly calendar updated Oct 30, 2026) and the SHMHA 2025 Minutes book (2025 minutes and 2026 directory). The Chattahoochee Convention has no 2025 minutes in the 2025-26 book; the 172nd session (2024) is verified. The Third Sunday Atlanta singing (Church of Our Saviour) conflicts between sources and is not counted. The African American note-singing circuit has a detailed schedule only for 2019 (last updated June 2019), with a single 2026 confirmation; it is excluded from totals. Open mics come mostly from one aggregator (Live Music Junkiez, updated Oct 21, 2026), so they are medium confidence, and 'folk-oriented' is my judgment. Bluegrass and Irish jams on that list belong to Layer 1 and are excluded. WRFG blocked scripted fetches (403), so the schedule came through a cached copy of its REST endpoint. AAFFM membership numbers are not published. The Great Southeast Music Hall's dates conflict (opened 1969 or 1972; MusicBrainz's 1976 closure is contradicted by the Pistols' 1978 show). Eddie's Attic founding: 1991 (venue) vs 1992 (Wikipedia and others). United Convention founding: 1904 vs 1905. Not verified or not found: 'Blue Llama' (no Atlanta venue found); Callanwolde folk programming; WABE or GPB weekly folk radio (none found); lined-out 'Dr. Watts' hymnody in metro churches (no 2024-26 evidence found); a regular ballad-singing circle (none found beyond events featuring Maggie Hunter). City Winery's site returned HTTP 429, so it is verified via search listings. House concerts are under-documented by design (private addresses). [atlanta-heritage] Research was done on Oct 30, 2026 with a shared, heavily rate-limited web_search tool, so breadth relied on direct fetches of organization sites, the ArtsATL / 285 South / Clarkston Community Center sites, the NEA fellows dataset (arcgis storymaps CSV, which ends at 2021) and New Georgia Encyclopedia. Search summaries hallucinated more than once and were corrected: a 'metro Atlanta' folklorico school was in Lemon Grove, CA, and a Georgia NEA list included non-fellows. Not verified or not found: son jarocho, bomba, Filipino rondalla, Hmong, Persian Nowruz music, Armenian music, youth mariachi programs, recent Georgia Council for the Arts apprenticeship recipients, Ethiopian/Eritrean music events beyond the 2025 Refugee Day venue, Igbo or Yoruba festivals, Bhutanese-Nepali dance groups (only general descriptions), current Black lined-hymn practice and gospel quartet anniversaries (almost no web footprint). Attendance numbers are mostly organizer or ticket-seller claims (Korean Festival 100,000; El Grito 60,000; Caribbean Carnival 60,000; JapanFest 20,000; garba 3,000-8,000 per night) and are low confidence. The Stone Mountain Highland Games' founding year conflicts (1972 per the Park and Atlanta Pipe Band; 1973 per the games' social handles; the 54th edition in 2026 fits 1973). The Korean American Association's festival page is internally inconsistent (founded 2009 yet '15th anniversary' in 2014). Some class schedules (KCC samulnori, Mirai Kanai practice) come from older pages. Annual events in recurring_events use per_month 0.083 so they don't inflate weekly counts; large multi-day festivals are in festivals only. Layer 1 items (Irish sessions, Scottish country dance classes, old-time and bluegrass jams) and Sacred Harp singings are left to the other slices. [atlanta-history] The shared web-search quota was exhausted for most of the session, so the research relied on direct fetches and DuckDuckGo. tunearch.org, atlantastudies.org, OCLC ArchiveGrid and arts.gov filtered lists blocked scripted access; some tune and archive facts rest on search snippets (medium confidence). Conflicts: Carson session date (June 14 per NGE vs. about June 19 per Smithsonian); WSB first broadcast (March 15 vs. 16, both NGE); AAFFM founding (1976 per AAFFM, 1980 incorporation, 1981 per ArtsATL); Great Southeast Music Hall dates (opened October 30, 1972 per Seal Place vs. 1969-1976 per MusicBrainz; closing late 1970s-early 1980s); Stokes injury (late 1920s vs. 1930); Carson's title count (3 per NGE vs. 7 per Play Bluegrass); Carson's birthplace and year; contra 50th (FB "2024" vs. AJC November 2025); McGraw's first singing (1952 vs. 1953); Lanierland opening (1970 vs. 1971). NEA fellows came from the NEA/Esri dataset (to 2021) plus AFS 2022-26 announcements; the Atlanta locations for Georgia Harris (likely an error) and the Blind Boys of Alabama are unverified. Unverified current status: the Phil Tanner Friday chicken-house jam, the Hiawassee Official State Fiddlers' Convention, the Blind Willie McTell Festival, the Falany festival's founding year, Stone Mountain Highland Games attendance. Gaps: no metro-specific documentation of Muscogee or Cherokee music or of named antebellum fiddlers; no fiddle-specialist shop; no current university fiddle or folk ensemble found; Atlanta Vintage Guitars unverified; Spalding County missing from the Maloy list.
